title: AI Writing Detectors Are Not Reliable and Often Generate Discriminatory False Positives
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard argues that schools relying on AI-text detectors are pursuing a lost cause, and lists seventeen reasons. Detectors produce both false positives and false negatives, cannot establish a threshold for how much AI text counts as cheating, and cannot prove authorship. They are biased against non-native English writers, are easily defeated by prompting, paraphrasing or personalization tools, and create adversarial classrooms. He warns administrators that known false positives expose them to lawsuits and urges schools to invest instead in teaching with AI and developing new assessment approaches. The post cites several studies and notes that institutions such as Vanderbilt have dropped the tools.
points: Detectors rest on patterns that are not reliably AI-specific, so false positives and negatives are unavoidable and fall hardest on non-native English writers.
There is no defensible threshold for how much AI-written text constitutes cheating, and no way to prove authorship.
Detection is easily defeated by prompting for style, paraphrasing, translation, or co-writing tools, so it mostly catches weaker students.
Constant scanning creates an adversarial relationship between teachers and students that undermines learning.
Schools should redirect money and time to training faculty to teach with AI and to new approaches to assessing writing.
quotes: (2) No detector predicts more than a probability of plagiarism. What’s your probability threshold for giving a student a failing grade or launching a plagiarism investigation?
(3) There is no way to determine what percentage of AI-text should be allowed. How much of the text must be artificial intelligence-written before it is considered cheating?

(4) There is no way to prove it. Large language models won’t ever reproduce the same exact text output twice; these aren’t databases! And even if they did, how would you prove a human didn’t also write it?

(8) It creates an adversarial classroom. If faculty are constantly scanning and checking individual papers for cheating, an adversarial relationship is created between teachers and students. This is magnified when a large number of false positives.

(16) They end up just punishing your already weaker students because the more advanced students just know more about playing the games. And the wealthier ones can just buy the new apps, such as conch.ai
Learning to write is still very important, but we need new approaches, not AI-writing detectors and punishments for suspected use.
